title: The call, time limits and lateness
summary: How you call for the target, how fast it must come, how much time you have in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, and what lateness costs.

body.html: A target does not fly by itself: you call for it with a short word such as 'pull' or 'ready'. The rules then set how fast the target must come and how much time you may take.
In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the clock runs from the referee's signal, in Compak® Sporting from your call; a target that comes too late is a No Bird.
body.heading: Watch the call and the release

body.html: Sporting™ keeps a steady rhythm, and several rules protect it. You call, and the referee relays your call to the trapper (the person who releases the targets) with a sound signal. From that signal, the target has to be in the air within 3 seconds. If it comes later, the referee calls a No Bird and the target is thrown again.

In Compak® Sporting a trap can be released by hand, with a remote control or by a sonopull (a microphone system that releases the trap when it hears your call). Released by hand, the target must leave 0 to 3 seconds after you call. A sonopull always waits half a second after your call, so the timing is the same each time. International events shot in line (shooters step onto station 1 one by one and move along the line to station 5) use sonopull only. A target that leaves more than 3 seconds late, or one you did not call for, is a No Bird.
In both disciplines the only target you may refuse is one you did not call for: it is a No Bird.

html.sporting: You may not refuse it. If it was thrown correctly and you do not fire, it is scored zero.
html.compak: You may not refuse it either. A refused single is scored zero; doubles follow the table in the rules guide.

html.sporting: You have at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles.
html.compak: You have at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target.

body.html: The first time you go over the limit, the referee gives a warning. After that, the red-card penalties apply (Chapter 12 · Red card on repeat at the same layout). When the referee has given a final decision, for example after you protested, you must carry on shooting within 15 seconds. If you do not, or if you stall on purpose, it counts as refusal to comply: a separate offence that the jury can sanction.

The first time you go over the limit, the referee notes a warning on the score sheet. If it happens again in the same round, it is a red card: a single is scored zero, and doubles follow the table in the rules guide (Chapter 21 · Penalty table after a first warning). When the referee has given a final decision, you must carry on shooting within 10 seconds. If you do not, or if you stall on purpose, it counts as refusal to comply, which the jury can sanction.

Many coaches suggest a short, steady pre-shot routine that fits well inside the limit. For example: step onto the stand, load when the referee allows it, take your ready position, breathe out, then call. More in Pre-shot routine: the same steps in the same order.

Lateness: if you are missing when your squad starts, the referee calls out your name and number, three times over one minute. If you arrive while the squad is still shooting the singles on the first stand and your turn has not yet passed, you join without penalty. After that, all targets you did not shoot are zeros, and you cannot make up the missed stands later with another squad.

If you were late for reasons outside your control, do not rejoin the squad in that round; appeal to the jury in writing. If the jury agrees, you shoot the round with another squad. If it refuses, each layout you did not shoot counts as 25 zeros.

In Compak® Sporting you must report to the referee in good time and confirm that you are there. Besides in line, there is the by-squad format: a squad of at most six shooters shoots the round together, moving from station to station. In this format, a shooter who arrives after the squad's first call of the round gets 25 zeros for that round. An appeal is made in writing to the jury, on the same day.

html.sporting: Be ready within 15 minutes of the call. If you are not there, you are disqualified.
html.compak: Be ready within 15 minutes of the call. If you are absent, you are treated as having withdrawn.

body.html: Put on hearing protection and glasses before you step onto the stand: in both disciplines a shooter without them is treated as absent (Dress code and safety on the stand).

notes.html: Do not hold the squad up with a long translation: keep it short now and give the details after the stand.

key_points.html: A target released more than 3 seconds late is a No Bird, in both disciplines.
You may not refuse a target you called for; one you did not call for is a No Bird.
Sporting™: at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles. Compak® Sporting: at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target.
Over the time limit, the first time brings a warning and a repeat brings a red card.
Be on time: in Sporting™ targets missed through lateness are zero; in Compak® Sporting by squad, coming after the squad's first call costs 25 zeros.

did_you_know.html: In Compak® Sporting in line you count as late once your number has been taken off in the scoring computer and the next shooter is already standing on station 1.

quiz.q: Within how many seconds of the call must the target be released?
quiz.explain: In both disciplines a target released more than 3 seconds late is a No Bird.

quiz.q: How long do you have to call in Compak® Sporting?
quiz.explain: You have at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target. In Sporting™ you have at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles.

quiz.q: A target is released although you did not call for it. What is it?
quiz.explain: A target you did not call for is a No Bird, and it is the only kind you may refuse.
